topics.topic: Sovereignty, Creation, and the Fall of Man
subtopics: God as the Creator and Preserver of the World
Creation account (Genesis 1 & 2)
The Fall of Man, consequences, and reconciliation (Genesis 3)
keypoints: Sovereignty of God: God is the supreme controller of the universe who creates ex nihilo (out of nothing) by His word and maintains all life.

Creation Accounts: Genesis 1 presents a systematic, six-day creation account culminating in humanity made in God's image. Genesis 2 emphasizes human responsibility, stewardship in Eden, and the institution of marriage.
Dignity and Mandate: Man was made in the image and likeness of God, given dominion over creation, and commanded to till and keep the garden.
The Fall of Man: Temptation by the serpent led to disobedience (eating from the tree of knowledge of good and evil), breaking the fellowship between God and humanity.
Consequences of Sin: Loss of innocence, spiritual and physical death, toil for man, pain in childbirth for woman, expulsion from Eden, and broken relationships.
God's Mercy: Even in judgment, God showed mercy by clothing Adam and Eve with animal skins and initiating a plan of redemption.

topics.topic: Leadership in Israel: Moses, Joshua, and the Judges
subtopics: Call and leadership of Moses (Exodus 3-14)
Leadership of Joshua and entry into Canaan (Joshua 1-6)
The era of Judges: Deborah, Gideon, and Samson
keypoints: Call of Moses: Called at the burning bush in Horeb to deliver Israel from Egyptian bondage; demonstrated God's personal name, Yahweh ('I AM WHO I AM').
The Exodus: Moses led Israel through plagues, the Passover, and the miraculous crossing of the Red Sea, highlighting God's power over human oppressors.
Joshua's Commission: Appointed as Moses' successor; exhorted to be strong, courageous, and obedient to the Law (Joshua 1:7-8); successfully led Israel across the Jordan into Canaan.
Conquest of Jericho: Demonstrates faith and obedience as central to Israel's military victories.
Cycle of the Judges: Israel's repeated pattern: Sin (apostasy) → Punishment (oppression by enemies) → Repentance (crying to God) → Redemption (God raises a Judge).
Key Judges: Deborah (faith and female leadership alongside Barak), Gideon (trust in God's strength over numbers), and Samson (consecrated Nazirite whose tragic flaw was compromise).

topics.topic: The Monarchy and Kingship in Israel
subtopics: Transition from Theocracy to Monarchy (1 Samuel 8-10)
Reigns of Saul, David, and Solomon
Division of the Kingdom (1 Kings 12)
keypoints: Transition to Monarchy: Israel demanded a human king 'like other nations,' rejecting God's direct rule (theocracy) through prophet Samuel.
King Saul: Israel's first king; initially humble, but failed through disobedience (unlawful sacrifice at Gilgal, sparing Agag and livestock of Amalek), leading to his rejection by God.
King David: Chosen as a man after God's own heart; united the tribes, established Jerusalem as political/religious capital, demonstrated true repentance (Psalm 51) after his sin with Bathsheba.
King Solomon: Blessed with wisdom and wealth; built the First Temple in Jerusalem; eventually led astray into idolatry through political marriages with foreign women.
Division of the Kingdom: Under Rehoboam (Solomon's son), heavy taxation and harsh counsel led to the split into Northern Kingdom (Israel under Jeroboam) and Southern Kingdom (Judah under Rehoboam).

topics.topic: Prophetic Concern for Social Justice and True Worship
subtopics: Amos: Social justice, righteousness, and true worship
Hosea: God's divine love and Israel's unfaithfulness
Isaiah: Call, holiness of God, and warning against religious formalism
keypoints: Prophet Amos: Ministered in the Northern Kingdom during a period of material prosperity and moral decay. Declared that God detests ritual worship devoid of justice: 'Let justice roll down like waters, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream' (Amos 5:24).
Amos' Denunciations: Condemned the oppression of the poor, corruption in courts, cheating in trade, and self-complacency of the wealthy.
Prophet Hosea: Used his tragic marriage to Gomer (an unfaithful wife) as a living parable of God's steadfast love (Hesed) for unfaithful Israel.
Hosea's Message: Emphasized that God desires steadfast love and knowledge of Him rather than sacrifice (Hosea 6:6).

Prophet Isaiah: Received a powerful vision of God's holiness in the temple (Isaiah 6). Warned Judah against trusting in empty religious rituals while committing social oppression and seeking foreign political alliances.

topics.topic: The Birth, Baptism, and Temptation of Jesus
subtopics: Annunciations and birth narratives (Matthew 1, Luke 1-2)
The ministry of John the Baptist
The Baptism and Temptation of Jesus (Matthew 3-4, Luke 3-4)
keypoints: Birth Narratives: Luke emphasizes the universal scope of salvation (angels appearing to humble shepherds), while Matthew focuses on the fulfillment of Old Testament prophecies (the Magi, flight to Egypt).
John the Baptist: Forerunner of the Messiah who preached a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins, fulfilling Isaiah's prophecy of a 'voice crying in the wilderness.'
Baptism of Jesus: Performed by John in River Jordan; signified Jesus' identification with humanity, divine approval ('This is my beloved Son'), and the inauguration of His public ministry.
Trinitarian Manifestation: The Father's voice, the Son being baptized, and the Holy Spirit descending like a dove.

Temptation of Jesus: Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness for 40 days to be tempted by Satan. He overcame every temptation (hedonism, materialism, presumption) by relying on the Scriptures ('It is written').

topics.topic: The Ministry and Teachings of Jesus Christ
subtopics: Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5-7)
Parables of the Kingdom of God
Miracles: Power over nature, disease, demons, and death
keypoints: Sermon on the Mount: Core ethical teaching of Jesus. The Beatitudes outline characteristics of Kingdom citizens. Jesus fulfilled the Law by addressing internal heart attitudes rather than mere external conformity (e.g., anger vs. murder, lust vs. adultery).

The Parables: Earthly stories with heavenly meanings used by Jesus to reveal Kingdom truths to receptive hearts while concealing them from the proud (e.g., Parable of the Sower, Prodigal Son, Good Samaritan).
Nature Miracles: Calming the storm and walking on water demonstrate Jesus' authority over physical creation.
Healing and Exorcism Miracles: Healing the paralytic, the woman with the issue of blood, and casting out legion of demons demonstrate compassion and victory over Satan's kingdom.
Raising the Dead: Raising Lazarus and the widow's son at Nain prove Jesus' supreme authority over physical death.

topics.topic: Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension of Jesus
subtopics: Triumphal Entry and the Last Supper
Arrest, Trial, Crucifixion, and Burial
Resurrection, Appearances, and Ascension
keypoints: Triumphal Entry: Jesus entered Jerusalem riding a donkey, fulfilling Zechariah 9:9 as the humble Prince of Peace.
The Last Supper: Reinterpreted the Passover feast; instituted the Lord's Supper (Holy Communion) representing His body broken and blood shed for the new covenant.
Agony in Gethsemane: Showed Jesus' authentic humanity and absolute submission to the Father's will ('Not my will, but yours be done').
Trial and Crucifixion: Betrayed by Judas, denied by Peter, falsely accused before the Sanhedrin and Pontius Pilate, and crucified at Golgotha as the sacrificial Lamb of God.
The Resurrection: Jesus rose bodily from the dead on the third day, demonstrating victory over sin and death, validated by the empty tomb and multiple eyewitness appearances.
The Ascension: Exaltation of Jesus into heaven 40 days post-resurrection, promising His return and commissioning disciples to evangelize the world.

topics.topic: The Early Church and the Holy Spirit
subtopics: The Day of Pentecost and the birth of the Church (Acts 2)
Communal living and growth of the early believers
Persecution, martyrdom of Stephen, and spread of the Gospel (Acts 6-8)
keypoints: Pentecost: Outpouring of the Holy Spirit on 120 believers in Jerusalem marked the birth of the Christian Church, empowering them with boldness and spiritual gifts.
Peter's Pentecost Sermon: Proclaimed the crucified and risen Jesus as Lord and Christ, leading to the conversion and baptism of about 3,000 souls.
Characteristics of the Early Church: Shared fellowship, breaking of bread, joint prayers, unity, and selling of possessions to care for the needy.
Appointment of Deacons: Seven men full of the Spirit and wisdom (including Stephen and Philip) were chosen to resolve administrative disputes in food distribution.
Persecution and Expansion: The martyrdom of Stephen triggered intense persecution in Jerusalem, which providentially scattered believers and spread the Gospel to Judea, Samaria, and beyond.

topics.topic: Missionary Journeys of Paul and the Jerusalem Council
subtopics: Conversion and call of Saul of Tarsus (Acts 9)
Paul's missionary journeys
The Jerusalem Council (Acts 15)
keypoints: Conversion of Paul: Saul, a zealous Pharisee persecuting Christians, encountered the risen Christ on the road to Damascus, leading to his transformation into the Apostle to the Gentiles.
First Missionary Journey: Paul and Barnabas preached across Cyprus and Asia Minor (Antioch in Pisidia, Lystra, Derbe), establishing churches despite strong opposition.
The Jerusalem Council (Acts 15): Convened to settle the Judaizing controversy—whether Gentile converts needed circumcision and adherence to the Mosaic Law for salvation.

Council's Ruling: Led by James and Peter, the council affirmed salvation by grace through faith alone for both Jews and Gentiles, requiring only abstinence from food offered to idols, blood, meat of strangled animals, and sexual immorality.
Subsequent Journeys: Paul expanded the Christian footprint into Europe (Philippi, Thessalonica, Athens, Corinth, and Ephesus).

topics.topic: Christian Living, Justification, and Fellowship in Epistles
subtopics: Justification by faith (Romans 3-5, Galatians 2-3)
Law and Grace
Christian interpersonal relationships, spiritual gifts, and civic duties
keypoints: Justification by Faith: Paul teaches that all humans have sinned and fall short of God's glory. Rightstanding with God cannot be earned through works of the Law, but is received as a free gift through faith in Jesus Christ.
Law vs. Grace: The Mosaic Law functions as a tutor/guardian to expose sin and point people to Christ, whereas Grace imparts the power to live a righteous life.
Spiritual Gifts (1 Corinthians 12-14): Bestowed by the Holy Spirit for the edification of the Church; must be exercised in order, humility, and above all, love (1 Corinthians 13).
Civic and Social Responsibilities: Christians are called to respect governing authorities (Romans 13), pay taxes, live peaceably with all men, and demonstrate genuine love.
Family and Work Ethics: Mutual submission, love between spouses, obedience of children to parents, and honesty between workers and employers (Ephesians 5-6).
